concepts.title: Semantic Versioning
concepts.description: A version number like 2.4.1 isn't just an incrementing label -- it's a promise about compatibility that consumers, and the tooling that automates their upgrades, rely on to decide whether pulling in a new release is safe without reading every line of its diff.
learningObjectives: State the MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH format and explain the specific compatibility promise each position is supposed to encode.
Explain why semantic versioning functions as a communication protocol between a package or service and its consumers, not merely a labeling convention.
Determine what counts as a breaking change based on the public contract affected, rather than the size of the underlying diff.
Explain how dependency version ranges (such as ^ and ~) mechanically rely on semver's promises being honored to resolve upgrades safely.
Diagnose the practical consequences when a breaking change is accidentally shipped as a MINOR or PATCH release.

sections.heading: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: A Promise, Not a Counter
sections.body:
Semantic versioning (semver) gives a version number three positions -- MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, like `2.4.1` -- and assigns each position a specific, agreed-upon meaning rather than treating the whole thing as an arbitrary incrementing label. Incrementing **PATCH** (2.4.1 -> 2.4.2) promises a backward-compatible bug fix: behavior that consumers rely on is unchanged, only something broken has been corrected. Incrementing **MINOR** (2.4.1 -> 2.5.0) promises backward-compatible new functionality: existing consumers keep working exactly as before, with something new now additionally available if they choose to use it. Incrementing **MAJOR** (2.4.1 -> 3.0.0) signals an incompatible change to the public contract -- something that existing consumers may need to update their own code to accommodate before upgrading safely.

The entire point of this scheme is to let a consumer decide, from the version number alone, roughly how much scrutiny an upgrade deserves -- without needing to read the full changelog or diff the entire release just to find out whether it's safe. A PATCH bump should be safe to pull in without a second thought; a MAJOR bump should be treated as 'stop and actually check what changed before upgrading.' That's a genuinely useful signal precisely because it's a promise made in advance, not a description applied after the fact -- a maintainer commits to what a given kind of bump will mean before anyone downstream has to trust it.

sections.heading: What Counts as 'Breaking' Is Defined by the Contract, Not the Diff Size
sections.body:
A natural but mistaken intuition is that a bigger change, or a change that took more effort, deserves a bigger version bump. Semantic versioning tracks something else entirely: impact on the **public contract** -- the surface a consumer actually depends on, whether that's a library's exported functions, an HTTP API's response shape, a CLI's flags, or a config file's schema. A single-line change that renames a JSON response field from `id` to `user_id` is a breaking change and warrants a MAJOR bump, even though the diff is one line, because every consumer parsing the old field name will now fail. Conversely, a sprawling internal rewrite -- replacing an entire algorithm, restructuring how a function is implemented internally -- can be entirely non-breaking, and therefore not even warrant a MINOR bump, if the function's inputs, outputs, and observable behavior are identical from the outside.

This means the first real discipline in applying semver correctly is being explicit about exactly what counts as your public contract in the first place -- which functions, fields, endpoints, or flags are consumer-facing commitments, and which are private implementation details you remain free to change without it counting as breaking anyone. A library that hasn't drawn this line clearly tends to either over-count internal refactors as breaking (bumping MAJOR far too often, training consumers to ignore the signal) or under-count real contract changes as trivial (bumping PATCH for something that actually breaks callers) -- both failures come from the same root cause: not having asked 'what, specifically, are we promising to keep stable here.'

sections.heading: Why Tooling and Automation Depend on the Promise Being Honored
sections.body:
Semver's usefulness isn't only about a human glancing at a changelog -- dependency managers mechanically encode trust in the promise through version range operators. A dependency declared as `^1.4.2` in a typical package manifest tells the tool 'automatically accept any version that is still compatible according to semver' -- which, for a version starting with a nonzero MAJOR, generally means any `1.x.y` release, since MINOR and PATCH bumps are supposed to be backward compatible by definition. A narrower `~1.4.2` restricts that to PATCH-level upgrades only. Automated dependency-update bots and routine `install`/`update` commands lean on exactly this mechanism to decide, with no human reviewing the specific change, whether it's safe to pull in a newer version.

If a maintainer ships a genuinely breaking change but only bumps the MINOR or PATCH number, every downstream project using a `^` or `~` range -- or any automated upgrade bot configured to auto-merge non-major bumps -- can silently pull in that breaking change and have it fail in CI, or worse, in production, with nobody having deliberately reviewed that specific change at all. This is the concrete, automation-facing reason semver discipline matters: it isn't only about being polite to human readers of a changelog, it's about not breaking the machinery that many consumers have explicitly configured to trust the version number's promise on their behalf.

sections.heading: Pre-1.0 and Pre-Release Versions: The Exception That Proves the Rule
sections.body:
Semver carves out an explicit exception for early development: a MAJOR version of `0` (like `0.4.2`) means the public contract is not yet considered stable, and anything -- including a breaking change -- may happen at any MINOR or PATCH bump, without violating the spec. This is precisely why `1.0.0` is meant to signal something specific: 'the public contract is now considered stable enough to make the normal compatibility promises about.' A common mistake is treating a long-lived `0.x` release as effectively stable just because it's been running in production for months or years -- the version number is explicitly telling consumers otherwise, and a maintainer is fully within the spec to ship a breaking change in `0.5.0 -> 0.6.0` precisely because that promise was never made in the first place.

Pre-release suffixes (`2.0.0-alpha`, `2.0.0-rc.1`) mark a version as not yet meeting even its own stated compatibility promise -- still subject to change before the final release. Build metadata (`1.4.2+build.17`) is different again: it identifies a specific build without affecting precedence or compatibility semantics at all, so `1.4.2+build.17` and `1.4.2+build.18` are considered the same version for comparison purposes. Both are worth recognizing precisely because they modify what the base version number would otherwise promise -- a pre-release tag downgrades the promise to 'not yet reliable,' while build metadata makes no compatibility claim whatsoever.

examples.title: Reading Three Different Version Bumps
examples.code:
1.4.2 -> 1.4.3   (PATCH)  "Fixed a null pointer exception in the export path."
1.4.2 -> 1.5.0   (MINOR)  "Added an optional `timeout` parameter to fetch()."
1.4.2 -> 2.0.0   (MAJOR)  "Removed the deprecated fetchSync() function."
examples.explanation: Each bump implies a different amount of action required from a consumer currently on `1.4.2`. The PATCH bump should be safe to accept with essentially no review -- it promises existing behavior is unchanged except for the specific fix. The MINOR bump is also safe to accept without any code changes -- the new `timeout` parameter is additive and optional, so anyone not using it sees no difference at all. The MAJOR bump requires an actual look: anyone still calling `fetchSync()` will break on upgrade and needs to migrate to whatever replaced it before taking this version. Reading just the version numbers, without opening a single changelog entry, already tells a consumer which of these three demands their attention.

examples.title: A One-Line Change That Is Still a MAJOR Bump
examples.explanation: The diff between these two responses is a single renamed key, but every existing consumer parsing this response by reading `response["id"]` will now get `None`/`undefined` and silently misbehave, or throw outright -- exactly the kind of consumer-facing break that MAJOR exists to flag loudly. Contrast this with a scenario where the API's internal database schema is completely restructured, table names changed, queries rewritten, but the JSON response emitted to consumers stays byte-for-byte identical -- that could legitimately ship as a PATCH, or no version bump beyond routine maintenance at all, despite involving a vastly larger amount of actual code change. The size of the diff and the size of the version bump are simply answering two different questions.

examples.title: A Version Range Trusting the Promise
examples.explanation: `^1.4.2` tells the package manager it may automatically resolve to any version from `1.4.2` up to, but not including, `2.0.0` -- covering `1.4.3`, `1.9.0`, or any other `1.x.y` release, on the assumption that every one of them honors semver's promise of staying backward compatible within the same MAJOR version. If the maintainer of `http-client` ships a genuinely breaking change but mistakenly tags it `1.5.0` instead of `2.0.0`, the next ordinary `npm install` in this project can pull that breaking release in automatically, with the declared range (`^1.4.2`) never having to change at all -- nothing in `package.json` looks any different, yet the installed dependency now behaves incompatibly. This is exactly the failure mode semver discipline exists to prevent: the range operator's safety depends entirely on version bumps meaning what they claim to mean.

misconceptions.description: A release that involved a lot of work, or a large code diff, deserves a bigger version bump -- for example, MAJOR for 'a lot of changes.'
misconceptions.clarification: Semantic versioning tracks impact on the public contract that consumers depend on, not effort or diff size. A massive internal rewrite that preserves every consumer-facing behavior exactly as it was is still, correctly, just a PATCH release (or no bump at all beyond routine maintenance) -- consumers were never exposed to any of that internal change. Meanwhile a single renamed public field, an easy one-line diff, is a MAJOR-worthy breaking change, because it invalidates an assumption every consumer parsing that field was relying on. The question semver answers is 'does upgrading require a consumer to check or change anything,' not 'how much did the maintainer do.'

misconceptions.description: Semantic versioning is really just a convention for humans reading changelogs -- it doesn't materially affect anything automated.
misconceptions.clarification: Dependency managers' range operators (`^`, `~`), lockfile resolution, and automated dependency-update bots mechanically trust the compatibility promise encoded in a version bump to decide, often with no human review at all, whether to pull in a new release. A `^1.4.2` range genuinely will auto-resolve to a later `1.x.y` release the moment one is published, with no human reading a changelog anywhere in that path. Violating the promise -- shipping a breaking change under a MINOR or PATCH bump -- causes real, automated breakage in downstream consumers' installs, builds, or production systems, not merely confusion for someone skimming release notes after the fact.

exercises.prompt: A maintainer is about to tag a new release. The current version is 2.3.0, and this release removes a public function that some consumers still call directly. They propose tagging it 2.3.1. Explain what's wrong with that choice and what it should be instead.
exercises.code:
# CHANGELOG.md (proposed)
## 2.3.1
- Removed the deprecated `formatLegacy()` export.

# proposed command:
# git tag v2.3.1 && npm publish
hints: A PATCH bump specifically promises that no consumer-facing behavior changes except for a fix -- does removing a function that consumers can still call fit that promise?
Think about what happens to any project that has `formatLegacy()` in active use and is pinned with a range like `^2.3.0` or `~2.3.0` -- would either range protect them from this specific change?
Removing a public export is an incompatible change to the contract, regardless of how small the removal itself looks in a diff -- that calls for a MAJOR bump, not a PATCH.
exercises.solutionCode:
# CHANGELOG.md (corrected)
## 3.0.0
- BREAKING: Removed the deprecated `formatLegacy()` export. Use `format()` instead.

# corrected command:
# git tag v3.0.0 && npm publish
exercises.solutionExplanation: Removing a still-callable public function is, by definition, an incompatible change to the library's public contract -- any consumer still calling `formatLegacy()` will break immediately on upgrading, with no code change of their own. A PATCH bump (2.3.0 -> 2.3.1) promises exactly the opposite: that nothing consumer-facing changes except for a corrected bug. Worse, a consumer pinned with `~2.3.0` (patch-only upgrades) or even `^2.3.0` (minor/patch upgrades) would have their tooling automatically accept this version with no warning at all, since both ranges are built on trusting that a non-major bump won't break them. Tagging this 3.0.0 instead correctly signals 'stop and check before upgrading,' and per-semver convention, `^2.3.0`-style ranges will not automatically resolve to a 3.x version at all, giving consumers the chance to review the breaking change deliberately before opting in.

exercises.prompt: A project's package.json declares "http-client": "^1.4.2". The package registry has published versions 1.4.2, 1.4.5, 1.9.0, and 2.0.0 of http-client. Running a fresh install today, which version does the package manager resolve to, and why not 2.0.0?
hints: `^1.4.2` means 'any version compatible with 1.4.2 according to semver' -- for a version whose MAJOR is nonzero, that generally means anything sharing the same MAJOR number.
Compare the MAJOR version of each published release against the MAJOR version in the declared range.
1.9.0 shares MAJOR version 1 with the declared 1.4.2; 2.0.0 does not.
exercises.expectedAnswer: It resolves to 1.9.0, the highest version matching ^1.4.2. 2.0.0 is excluded because ^ restricts upgrades to the same MAJOR version as the declared range (here, MAJOR version 1) -- 2.0.0 has a different MAJOR version and is assumed, by the semver promise, to potentially be incompatible, so the package manager will never select it automatically under this range.
exercises.solutionExplanation: `^1.4.2` is interpreted as 'anything from 1.4.2 up to, but not including, 2.0.0,' which is exactly the range of versions semver promises will remain backward compatible with 1.4.2. Among the published versions, 1.4.5 and 1.9.0 both fall within that range, and the package manager resolves to the highest matching one, 1.9.0, to get the most up-to-date compatible release. 2.0.0 sits outside the range specifically because it carries a different MAJOR number, which by definition may include incompatible changes -- accepting it automatically would defeat the entire purpose of declaring a `^` range in the first place, since the consumer would be silently exposed to changes semver never promised would be safe.

assessments.prompt: A library's maintainers rewrite the entire internal implementation of a function -- new algorithm, new internal data structures, hundreds of changed lines -- but its exported signature, inputs, outputs, and observable behavior remain identical to consumers. According to semantic versioning, what version bump does this warrant?
options: A MAJOR bump, because the amount of code that changed is substantial.
At most a PATCH bump (or no version-relevant bump at all), because semver tracks changes to the public contract, and this change is entirely invisible to consumers.
A MINOR bump, since any meaningful engineering effort should be reflected in the version number.
It cannot be determined without knowing exactly how many lines of code changed.
assessments.explanation: Semver's bump categories are defined entirely in terms of the public contract's compatibility, not the size or effort of the underlying change. Since every consumer-observable aspect of the function -- its signature, inputs, outputs, and behavior -- is unchanged, this qualifies as at most a PATCH-level change (commonly bundled as a general internal improvement with no dedicated bump at all), regardless of how large the internal diff is. Option A and C both mistake diff size or effort for contract impact, which is precisely the misconception this concept addresses; option D is a distractor implying line count is the deciding factor, when it is specifically not what semver measures.

assessments.prompt: A dependency is declared as ~2.3.1 in a project's manifest. According to this concept, which upgrades will this range operator automatically accept?
options: Any version from 2.3.1 up to, but not including, 3.0.0 -- the exact same range as ^2.3.1.
Only PATCH-level upgrades on top of 2.3.1, such as 2.3.2 or 2.3.5, but not MINOR or MAJOR bumps -- ~ restricts upgrades to PATCH-level only, a narrower range than ^.
Any version at all, including releases in the 3.x or 4.x line, since ~ means 'approximately compatible.'
No automatic upgrades whatsoever -- ~ pins the dependency to exactly version 2.3.1 with no flexibility.
assessments.explanation: The concept explicitly distinguishes the two operators: `^1.4.2` allows any compatible MINOR or PATCH release within the same MAJOR version, while `~1.4.2` restricts that further to PATCH-level upgrades only. Option A conflates the two distinct operators the concept deliberately contrasts. Option C vastly overstates what ~ permits. Option D ignores that ~ does allow some automatic upgrading, just a narrower range than ^.

assessments.prompt: A library has been running in production for two years at version 0.6.3, and a maintainer ships a breaking change in the jump to 0.7.0. According to this concept, does this violate semantic versioning?
options: Yes -- any breaking change always requires a MAJOR version bump, with absolutely no exceptions under the spec.

No -- semver explicitly carves out an exception for a MAJOR version of 0, meaning the public contract is not yet considered stable, and a breaking change may happen at any MINOR or PATCH bump without violating the spec, regardless of how long the library has actually been running in production.
Yes, because the library has clearly been stable enough in real-world practice to have earned normal semver protections by now.
No, but only because 0.7.0 happens to be an odd-numbered MINOR version rather than an even one.
assessments.explanation: The concept states this exception directly: a MAJOR version of 0 means the contract isn't yet considered stable, and this is precisely why 1.0.0 is meant to signal that the compatibility promise begins -- production usage duration doesn't change what the version number itself promises. Option A ignores the explicit 0.x exception the concept describes. Option C substitutes real-world usage for the version number's own stated promise, which the concept explicitly warns against. Option D invents an irrelevant even/odd distinction that has no basis in semver.

assessments.prompt: An automated dependency-update bot is configured to auto-merge any MINOR or PATCH version bump without human review, trusting that such bumps are backward compatible by definition. What specific risk does this configuration carry, according to this concept?
options: No real risk -- MINOR and PATCH bumps are guaranteed by the tooling itself to never break anything, regardless of what the maintainer actually shipped.

If a maintainer ships a genuinely breaking change but mislabels it as a MINOR or PATCH bump, the bot will auto-merge it with no human review at all, since the entire mechanism depends on the version bump honestly reflecting what actually changed.
The bot will always catch breaking changes regardless of how they're labeled, since it inspects the actual code diff before merging.
This configuration only carries risk for MAJOR version bumps, which is precisely why those are excluded from auto-merge.
assessments.explanation: The concept makes this exact point about automation trusting the promise: a `^` or `~` range, and any bot configured to auto-merge on that basis, will pull in a mislabeled breaking change with no human review, because the mechanism's safety depends entirely on the version bump meaning what it claims. Option A wrongly assumes tooling itself enforces correctness, when it only enforces the range rule. Option C invents inspection behavior the bot does not perform. Option D misses that the actual risk lies with MINOR/PATCH bumps specifically, which is exactly why they're the ones auto-merged without review.

assessments.prompt: A team ships a change that removes a deprecated CLI flag, tagging the release as a PATCH bump because 'it was just cleanup and the flag was already marked deprecated.' Within a week, several downstream teams' automated deployment pipelines start failing. Explain what went wrong and what should have happened instead.
assessments.modelAnswer: Marking a flag as deprecated is a signal of *intent* to remove it eventually -- it is not the same event as actually removing it, and semver cares specifically about the removal itself, not about whether a warning preceded it. The moment the flag stops being accepted at all, any consumer -- human or, in this case, an automated deployment pipeline -- that still passes that flag will fail outright, which is exactly the definition of a breaking change to the CLI's public contract (its set of supported flags). Tagging this as a PATCH violates the specific promise a PATCH bump makes: that nothing consumer-facing changes except for a corrected defect. The downstream failures are a direct, mechanical consequence of that violation: many of those pipelines were almost certainly configured with a dependency range like `^` or `~` on this tool, or simply ran an unconditional 'always take the latest patch' update step, precisely because a PATCH bump is supposed to be safe to accept automatically with no review -- the whole point of that convention is to let exactly this kind of unattended, automatic upgrade happen without incident. What should have happened instead is tagging this release as a MAJOR bump, with the removal explicitly called out in the changelog (ideally with a migration note, e.g. 'use --new-flag instead'), which would have caused any range-pinned consumer's tooling to correctly decline to auto-upgrade, giving each downstream team the chance to review and update deliberately before adopting the new version, rather than being broken by an update their own automation believed was guaranteed safe.

concepts.title: Feature Flags: Decoupling Deployment from Release
concepts.description: Deploying code and releasing a feature are two different events, and feature flags are the mechanism that lets a team choose to separate them on purpose -- but flags come in several genuinely different flavors with different lifetimes and failure modes, and treating them all the same is itself a common source of both bugs and quietly accumulating technical debt.
learningObjectives: Define deployment and release as distinct events, and explain precisely what mechanism feature flags provide to decouple them.
Distinguish release toggles, ops toggles (kill switches), experiment toggles, and permission toggles by purpose and expected lifetime.
Explain why a kill switch has different design and testing requirements than a gradual-rollout release toggle, particularly regarding reliability under failure.
Explain the combinatorial testing burden multiple simultaneous feature flags introduce, and how teams manage it.
Design a flag lifecycle policy, including ownership and retirement, that prevents flag debt from accumulating silently.

sections.heading: Deployment Is Not Release: Two Separate Events, on Purpose
sections.body:
**Deployment** is the event where code physically starts running in a production environment. **Release** is the separate event where a feature actually becomes visible or active for some set of real users. Without a feature flag, these two events are forced to happen at the same instant -- the moment the deploy completes, the new behavior is simply live for everyone, whether or not that was actually the intended timing. A feature flag is the specific mechanism that breaks that forced coupling: code guarded by a flag can be deployed to production while the flag remains off, meaning the deployment has happened but the release deliberately has not.

The practical payoff is that deployment becomes a low-risk, frequent, easily reversible event -- since a dormant flag means nothing user-visible changes, there's very little at stake in deploying often -- while release becomes its own deliberate decision, one that can be timed, targeted to a subset of users, ramped up gradually, or flipped back off instantly, all without touching the deployment pipeline again. This is the release-engineering framing of the same mechanism introduced in the Branching Models module: there, the emphasis was on how flags let trunk-based development merge incomplete work safely; here, the emphasis is on treating 'is it deployed' and 'is it released' as two independently controllable questions, which turns out to matter for several different, more specialized uses of flags than just gating one in-progress feature.

sections.heading: A Taxonomy of Flags: They're Not All the Same Tool
sections.body:
'Feature flag' is used as an umbrella term for several genuinely different tools, distinguished mainly by expected lifetime and purpose -- conflating them is where a lot of avoidable flag-related trouble comes from.

**Release toggles** gate an in-progress or newly-finished feature; they're meant to be short-lived, existing only from when the feature starts merging to trunk until it's fully rolled out and confirmed stable, at which point the toggle and the old code path it guarded should both be deleted.

**Ops toggles**, often called **kill switches**, control operational behavior rather than gating a specific feature's rollout -- for example, a switch that instantly disables an expensive or currently-misbehaving subsystem under load. These are meant to be long-lived, flipped rarely, and -- critically -- must work reliably under exactly the pressure of an active incident, which imposes design requirements the other categories don't share.

**Experiment toggles** power A/B tests, routing different users to different variants and tying that assignment to analytics; they're retired once the experiment concludes and a winning variant is chosen, similar in lifetime to a release toggle but tied to a measurement process rather than a rollout process.

**Permission toggles** gate functionality by plan, tier, or entitlement -- 'is this account on the Enterprise plan,' 'does this user have the beta-features role enabled.' Unlike the other three categories, these are meant to be permanent: they encode ongoing business logic, not a temporary rollout decision, and applying 'delete once fully rolled out' thinking to a permission toggle is a mistake, since there is no rollout to complete -- the toggle's condition is meant to keep varying by account indefinitely.

sections.heading: The Hidden Cost: Combinatorial Test Surface and Kill-Switch Reliability
sections.body:
Every independent flag that can be either on or off effectively doubles the number of meaningfully distinct states the system as a whole can be in. Two flags together imply four combinations; three imply eight -- and untested combinations, particularly where one flag's new code path calls into another flag's new code path, are exactly where subtle bugs hide, since each flag was very possibly tested carefully in isolation but never in combination with the other. Teams manage this cost in a few concrete ways: keeping the number of concurrently active *temporary* flags (release and experiment toggles) deliberately small, explicitly testing both states of any flag on a critical path rather than assuming 'it worked with it off, it'll work with it on,' and being honest that exhaustive combination testing doesn't scale -- which is itself a strong argument for keeping temporary flag lifetimes short, since the combinatorial surface only exists for as long as the flag does.

Kill switches carry an additional, sharper reliability requirement that the other categories don't: a kill switch must keep working under precisely the conditions it exists to respond to, which usually means an already-degraded or overloaded system. A kill switch whose own on/off state is read from the very database or service that's currently struggling is a dangerously circular design -- the one moment you most need to flip it is exactly the moment that lookup is most likely to also be slow or failing. Kill-switch state is generally worth storing in a separate, simpler, independently highly-available store specifically so that flipping it doesn't depend on the health of the thing it's meant to control.

sections.heading: Flag Lifecycle and Retiring Flags
sections.body:
A release or experiment toggle's life has a natural shape: introduced, off by default; gradually enabled for a growing percentage of users (mirroring canary-style rollout, covered in the Branching Models module); fully enabled for everyone; confirmed stable through a soak period with no need to flip it back off; and finally, the flag check and the old code path it replaced are both deleted. The last step is the one most often skipped under time pressure, because once a flag is at 100% and nothing is visibly wrong, there's little urgency pushing anyone to go back and remove it -- which is exactly how flag debt accumulates: a codebase slowly fills with permanent branching logic for decisions that were actually settled months or years earlier, and every future reader of that code has to mentally parse a conditional whose 'off' branch will genuinely never execute again.

A concrete mitigation, similar in spirit to a postmortem's action items needing an owner and a due date, is assigning each temporary flag an owner and an expected review or expiration date at the moment it's created -- not as an afterthought once someone notices it's overdue. A flag that's been sitting at 100% for months with no owner actively tracking its removal is a reliable, visible signal of quietly accumulating technical debt, worth treating with the same seriousness as an old, forgotten TODO comment -- except that unlike a TODO, a live flag also keeps the full combinatorial test-surface cost from the previous section paid indefinitely, for a decision that was already made.

examples.title: Deployment and Release as Genuinely Separate Events
examples.explanation: The code deploys once, on Tuesday, and never needs to be touched again for the rest of this timeline -- every subsequent change in what users actually experience (10% on Thursday, 100% the following Monday) happens purely by flipping the flag's configuration, with no new deployment, no new build, and no new artifact involved at all. This is deployment and release fully decoupled: Tuesday's deploy was a low-stakes, easily-reversible event precisely because nothing user-visible changed as a result of it, while Thursday's and Monday's actual release decisions were made independently, on a schedule driven by business judgment and observed metrics rather than by whenever the next deploy happened to land.

examples.title: Four Flags, Four Different Lifecycles
examples.code:
flags:
  - name: new_checkout_flow
    type: release
    owner: priya
    created: 2026-07-01
    review_by: 2026-09-01     # delete flag + legacy path by this date once at 100%

  - name: disable_recommendation_engine
    type: ops
    owner: on-call-rotation
    created: 2025-11-12
    review_by: null            # permanent -- this is a kill switch, not a rollout

  - name: pricing_experiment_q3
    type: experiment
    owner: growth-team
    created: 2026-07-15
    review_by: 2026-08-30      # retire once the experiment concludes

  - name: enterprise_sso
    type: permission
    owner: platform-team
    created: 2025-03-01
    review_by: null            # permanent -- encodes plan entitlement, not a rollout
examples.explanation: Each flag's `type` field drives a genuinely different expectation. `new_checkout_flow` and `pricing_experiment_q3` both have a concrete `review_by` date, because they represent temporary states that are supposed to resolve -- either full rollout or experiment conclusion -- after which the flag should be deleted. `disable_recommendation_engine` and `enterprise_sso` both have `review_by: null` deliberately, not because nobody got around to setting a date, but because neither one is ever supposed to be 'finished': the kill switch needs to remain available indefinitely as an operational safety valve, and the permission toggle needs to keep varying by account forever, since new customers will keep signing up for and canceling the Enterprise plan long after this flag was created. Treating all four the same -- for instance, scheduling `enterprise_sso` for deletion the way `new_checkout_flow` is -- would be a straightforward, avoidable mistake.

examples.title: A Kill Switch That Depends on the Thing It's Meant to Disable
examples.explanation: In the broken version, if the recommendation engine is degrading performance specifically by putting excessive load on the primary database, checking the kill switch requires querying that same overloaded database -- meaning the exact moment an on-call engineer most needs to flip this switch and have it take effect is also the moment that lookup is most likely to be slow or timing out. The fixed version stores kill-switch state in an independent, deliberately simple and highly-available store -- separate infrastructure, minimal dependencies of its own -- specifically so that reading and flipping it doesn't depend on the health of whatever it's meant to control. This is a design requirement fairly specific to kill switches: a release toggle gating a new checkout flow doesn't need this level of independence, because nothing about checking it is expected to happen during an active incident involving the checkout flow's own dependencies being down.

misconceptions.description: All feature flags are basically the same thing, and every flag should be deleted once the feature it gates is fully rolled out.
misconceptions.clarification: That expectation is correct for release toggles and experiment toggles, which exist specifically to manage a temporary rollout or experiment and should indeed be deleted once it concludes. It is incorrect for permission toggles, which encode ongoing, permanent business logic (like plan entitlement) with no rollout to ever complete, and largely incorrect for ops toggles/kill switches, which are meant to persist indefinitely as a standing operational safety valve. Applying a blanket 'delete after full rollout' policy without first identifying which category a given flag belongs to risks either deleting permanent business logic by mistake, or -- just as commonly -- never scheduling genuinely temporary flags for removal because nobody distinguished them from the permanent ones in the first place.

misconceptions.description: Once a flag is flipped to 100% for all users, the work related to that flag is done.
misconceptions.clarification: Reaching 100% means the *release* decision is complete -- the feature is now live for everyone -- but it does not mean the *engineering* cleanup is complete. The old code path the flag used to fall back to, the flag check itself, and any now-unused configuration ideally still need to be removed, typically after a short soak period to confirm stability at full rollout. Skipping this step is exactly how flag debt accumulates: the flag becomes a permanent fixture in the codebase for a decision that was, in reality, settled long ago, and every future engineer reading that code still has to mentally parse a branch that will genuinely never take its 'off' path again.

exercises.prompt: A recommendation service occasionally becomes slow enough to drag down page load times across the whole site. You're asked to add a kill switch that on-call engineers can flip to instantly stop calling it (falling back to a simple default list) during an incident. Write the flag-check logic, and explain where its state should live and why.
hints: This is an ops toggle / kill switch, not a release toggle -- think about what's different about when and under what conditions it needs to actually work.
If the recommendation engine's own slowness is caused by load on a shared database, would storing the kill switch's state in that same database be a safe choice?
The switch needs to be readable and flippable reliably even while the system it controls is actively struggling -- that points toward a separate, simple, independently available store.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The check itself is intentionally simple -- a kill switch's logic should be as close to foolproof as possible, since it's meant to be trusted during an active incident. The important design decision is where `kill_switch_cache` actually lives: it must be a store independent of the recommendation engine and whatever shared infrastructure (like a primary database under load) might be causing the slowness in the first place. If the switch's own state were stored in that same struggling system, flipping it during an incident could be exactly as slow or unreliable as the problem it's meant to solve -- a circular dependency that defeats the purpose of having a kill switch at all. A small, dedicated, highly-available key-value store with minimal dependencies of its own is the standard choice, precisely because it needs to keep working when almost everything else might not be.

exercises.prompt: This flag registry has a scheduling mistake that would cause a problem in a few weeks. Find and fix it.
exercises.code:
flags:
  - name: dark_mode_rollout
    type: release
    owner: maria
    review_by: 2026-09-10

  - name: enterprise_sso
    type: permission
    owner: platform-team
    review_by: 2026-09-15   # scheduled for deletion once "complete"
hints: Compare the `type` field of each flag against what a `review_by` date scheduled for deletion actually implies.
One of these flags gates a temporary rollout; the other encodes ongoing plan entitlement that never actually finishes rolling out to 'everyone,' since new accounts keep signing up over time.
Permission toggles generally shouldn't have a deletion date at all -- what should `enterprise_sso`'s entry look like instead?
exercises.solutionCode:
flags:
  - name: dark_mode_rollout
    type: release
    owner: maria
    review_by: 2026-09-10

  - name: enterprise_sso
    type: permission
    owner: platform-team
    review_by: null   # permanent -- encodes ongoing plan entitlement, never "complete"
exercises.solutionExplanation: `enterprise_sso` is a permission toggle: it decides whether a given account currently has the Enterprise plan's SSO feature enabled, which is a check that needs to keep working for every future account indefinitely, not a temporary rollout with a finish line. Scheduling it for deletion on 2026-09-15 as if it were a release toggle would eventually cause the flag (and the entitlement check it performs) to be removed entirely, which would either accidentally grant SSO to every account regardless of plan, or break it for every Enterprise account, depending on what the code defaults to once the check is gone -- either way, a real production incident caused purely by a scheduling mistake in the flag registry, not by any code change. `dark_mode_rollout`, by contrast, is correctly a release toggle with a real deletion date, since it's meant to be retired once the rollout is confirmed stable.

assessments.prompt: A team stores a kill switch's on/off state in the same primary database that the subsystem it's meant to disable also depends on heavily. What is the specific risk this creates?
options: There is no real risk, since any working database read is fast enough for this purpose.
If that subsystem's load is what's degrading the database, checking or flipping the kill switch may itself become slow or unreliable at exactly the moment it's most needed.
The risk is purely about cost -- storing flag state in a primary database is more expensive than using a dedicated flag service.
This only matters if the kill switch is checked on every single request rather than cached.
assessments.explanation: The core danger is a circular dependency: a kill switch exists specifically to be flipped when something is going wrong, and if the thing going wrong is degrading the very store the switch's own state lives in, reading or writing that state can become just as slow or unreliable as the problem it's meant to address -- undermining the switch exactly when it matters most. Option A ignores this failure mode entirely. Option C raises a real but secondary concern (cost) that isn't the specific operational risk being tested here. Option D describes an unrelated performance detail that doesn't change the fundamental circularity problem, which exists regardless of caching strategy.

assessments.prompt: Code guarded by a feature flag is deployed to production on Tuesday with the flag off, then the flag is flipped on for 10% of users the following Thursday, with no new deployment happening in between. According to this concept, what does this timeline illustrate?
options: A bug -- the feature should have been fully visible to all users the moment it was deployed on Tuesday.

Deployment and release as genuinely separate events -- the code physically started running on Tuesday (deployment) while the feature only became visible to any real users on Thursday (release), decoupled entirely by the flag's runtime state rather than by any new deploy.
A canary deployment specifically, since it involves gradually increasing traffic percentages over time.
Evidence that the CI/CD pipeline is broken, since deploying and releasing should always happen at the exact same moment.
assessments.explanation: The concept's opening framing is exactly this: deployment is the event where code starts running, release is the separate event where a feature becomes visible to users, and a feature flag is what breaks the forced coupling between the two. Option A assumes the coupling the concept says flags exist to break. Option C mislabels a feature-flag rollout as a deployment strategy, which is a related but distinct mechanism covered elsewhere. Option D treats intentional decoupling as if it were a malfunction.

assessments.prompt: A team applies a blanket policy that every feature flag must be deleted once it reaches 100% enablement. What problem does this policy create for a permission toggle like enterprise_sso, according to this concept?
options: No problem -- permission toggles should indeed be deleted once every existing customer has the Enterprise plan enabled.

A permission toggle encodes ongoing, permanent business logic (plan entitlement) with no rollout to ever complete, since new accounts keep signing up over time -- deleting it under a 'fully rolled out' policy would remove entitlement logic that's meant to keep varying by account indefinitely.
The policy is fine specifically for permission toggles, since they are the one category explicitly meant to be deleted the fastest.
Permission toggles are never affected by any deletion policy at all, since they technically cannot be set to 100% enablement.
assessments.explanation: The concept explicitly warns against this blanket policy, noting that permission toggles are meant to be permanent because they encode ongoing business logic with no rollout to complete, unlike release and experiment toggles. Option A misapplies rollout-completion thinking to a category that has no rollout to complete. Option C reverses which categories are meant to be short-lived versus permanent. Option D is factually incorrect -- a permission toggle can absolutely reach a state where it applies broadly, it just never 'finishes' in the way a release toggle does.

assessments.prompt: A team has five independent feature flags simultaneously active, all gating pieces of the same feature area, and tests each flag only in isolation with the other four left at their default state. According to this concept, what risk does this testing approach leave unaddressed?
options: None -- if each flag works correctly on its own, the combination of all five is mathematically guaranteed to also work correctly.

Five independent binary flags imply thirty-two distinct system states; a bug caused specifically by an interaction between two flags' code paths would never surface from testing each flag alone with the others left off, since that specific combination was never actually exercised.
The only risk is a performance slowdown caused by checking too many flags on a single request.
This risk only applies to release toggles specifically; permission and ops toggles are exempt from any combinatorial testing risk.
assessments.explanation: The concept states this combinatorial cost explicitly: every independent flag doubles the number of meaningfully distinct system states, and untested combinations -- especially where one flag's new code path calls into another's -- are exactly where subtle bugs hide. Option A assumes independence that the concept explicitly says doesn't generally hold, especially for flags gating the same feature area. Option C substitutes an unrelated performance concern for the actual correctness risk described. Option D fabricates an exemption the concept never states -- the combinatorial mechanism applies to any set of simultaneously active flags.

assessments.prompt: A teammate wants to add five new feature flags simultaneously for an upcoming release, all gating pieces of the same new checkout redesign, and says testing 'each flag on its own' should be sufficient. Explain the risk in this plan and what you'd recommend instead.
assessments.modelAnswer: Testing each flag in isolation only verifies that each individual piece works correctly when every other flag is in its default state -- it says nothing about the states that actually matter once all five flags exist simultaneously in production, where they can independently be on or off in any combination. Five independent binary flags imply thirty-two distinct system states, and a bug specifically caused by an interaction -- flag A's new code path calling into, or making an assumption that's only true when, flag B's new code path is active -- would never surface from testing each flag one at a time with the others left off, precisely because that specific combination was never actually exercised. This risk is compounded by the fact that all five flags gate pieces of the same checkout redesign, meaning they're unusually likely to interact with each other's code paths rather than being genuinely independent, which makes the untested-combination risk higher here than it would be for five unrelated flags scattered across different parts of the system. Rather than trying to exhaustively test all thirty-two combinations, which doesn't scale and isn't realistic under a normal release timeline, I'd recommend two things: first, wherever practical, consolidate tightly related flags into fewer, coarser-grained ones -- if these five pieces are always meant to ship and roll back together as one redesign, a single `new_checkout_redesign` flag removes the combinatorial problem entirely by construction. Second, for whatever flags remain genuinely independent, prioritize testing the specific combinations that are plausible in production (all five off, all five on, and any partial states the rollout plan will actually pass through), rather than assuming isolated single-flag tests generalize to combinations that were never run. Keeping these flags' collective lifetime short and getting them fully rolled out and deleted quickly also limits how long this combinatorial risk has to actually matter.

concepts.title: Rollback Strategies and the Database Problem
concepts.description: Rolling back stateless application code is often just redeploying the previous immutable artifact -- cheap, fast, mechanical. Rolling back once a database migration is involved is fundamentally harder, because a database has no automatic 'previous version' the way a versioned artifact does, and understanding why is what separates a rollback plan that actually works from one that causes a second outage on top of the first.
learningObjectives: Explain why rolling back stateless application code is comparatively easy, and identify exactly what property of immutable, versioned artifacts makes it so.
Explain the expand-contract migration pattern and why it exists specifically to keep two versions of application code simultaneously compatible with one evolving schema.
Diagnose a scenario where rolling back application code alone, without accounting for an already-applied migration, causes new errors or data corruption.
Compare roll-back and roll-forward as incident response strategies and identify the conditions under which each is the safer choice.
Design a rollback-safe release plan for a change that includes both application code and a database migration.

sections.heading: Why Code Rollback Is (Comparatively) Easy
sections.body:
The CI/CD module established two ideas that combine to make rolling back stateless application code cheap: artifacts are built once, tagged immutably, and promoted unchanged through every environment; and, in a blue-green setup, the previous version is never torn down during a cutover, so rollback is just pointing the router back at it. Put together, rolling back a stateless service is mechanically simple: stop routing traffic to (or stop running) the new version, and resume routing to (or restart) the exact same immutable artifact that was running successfully before. There is no reconstruction involved -- the previous version's bytes still exist, unchanged, ready to run exactly as they did a moment ago.

This works cleanly specifically *because* a stateless process carries no persisted memory of its own between requests -- kill it, start the old version, and from the process's own point of view nothing has been lost, because there was nothing stored in it to lose. That specific property -- no persisted state inside the thing being rolled back -- is the load-bearing assumption behind describing rollback as fast and mechanical, and it's exactly the assumption that breaks the moment a database is involved.

sections.heading: Why State Breaks the Simple Story
sections.body:
A database does not have a 'previous version' in the sense an artifact does. There is exactly one current set of rows and one current schema, continuously mutating, with no separate, preserved copy of 'the schema and data as they existed five minutes ago' sitting alongside it the way a blue environment sits alongside green. If a migration has already run -- adding a column, changing a type, backfilling values, dropping a column -- before a bad release is caught, redeploying the previous application artifact does not undo that migration. The schema is still in its new shape; only the application code has reverted.

Concretely: suppose a release adds a `price_cents` column with a `NOT NULL` constraint and no default, and the new application code is updated to populate it on every insert. The release turns out to have an unrelated bug, and the team rolls back to the previous application version. That previous version's `INSERT` statements were written before this column existed, so they don't populate `price_cents` at all -- but the constraint requiring a value is still there, because the schema never rolled back. The result is that the rollback, which was supposed to be the safe, fast fix, itself starts causing every insert to fail -- an outage caused directly by the act of rolling back, on code that was previously running perfectly well, simply because the database underneath it is no longer in the shape that old code assumes.

sections.heading: Expand-Contract: Making Two Versions of Code Compatible With One Schema
sections.body:
The **expand-contract** (or parallel change) pattern exists specifically to keep both the old and new application code able to run correctly against the database during the window where either one might be active. It has three distinct phases, and the discipline is in not collapsing them together.

**Expand**: add new schema elements alongside the old ones, without removing anything yet -- add `price_cents` as *nullable*, with application code updated to dual-write both the legacy `price` field and the new `price_cents` field, and backfill historical rows in the background. At this point, both old code (which only knows about `price`) and new code (which writes both) can run against this schema without error.

**Migrate**: deploy application code that reads from and relies on the new `price_cents` column, while it's still present and still being kept correct by dual-writes. If a rollback to the previous version is needed during this phase, that previous version still works, because `price` is still there, still populated, and the schema never removed anything it depended on.

**Contract**: only once there's real confidence -- a soak period with no rollback need, several successful deploys behind the change -- remove the old `price` column and stop dual-writing, finally converging on `price_cents` alone. This is the phase that actually removes the safety net: once `price` is gone, the previous application version can no longer run correctly against this schema, and rollback of code alone stops being a real option again, exactly as it was before this pattern was applied. The entire value of expand-contract is in how long the window between migrate and contract is deliberately kept open, not in rushing through all three phases back to back.

sections.heading: Roll Back vs Roll Forward
sections.body:
**Rollback** means reverting to the previous known-good version. **Roll forward** means shipping a new, corrective change on top of the current (bad) version, rather than reverting to an earlier one. For purely stateless issues caught before any migration has reached its contract phase, rollback is usually the faster and safer choice -- it's mechanical, well-understood, and doesn't require writing and reviewing a new fix under incident pressure.

But once a migration has done something irreversible -- dropped a column that a rollback target's code still expects, run a destructive backfill that overwrote or discarded the previous representation of the data -- rollback is not simply riskier, it can be outright impossible without a real, separate data-recovery effort: the old code's assumptions about the schema are no longer true, and there is no 'undo' for a dropped column short of restoring from a backup, which carries its own risk of losing other data written since. In exactly that situation, roll-forward is usually the only realistic path: ship a targeted fix on top of the current schema and code, because reverting to a version that no longer matches reality would create a second, likely worse, incident on top of the first. The decision in the moment generally comes down to a concrete question: has this specific migration already passed the point of no return (contract-phase-style, irreversible changes), and if so, is a quick forward fix genuinely available, or is the team about to discover that neither direction is actually safe -- which is precisely the scenario a rollback plan should have ruled out before the release ever shipped, not during the incident itself.

sections.heading: Designing the Rollback Plan Before You Need It
sections.body:
The practical discipline is asking, before any release that includes a schema change, a specific question: 'if we need to roll back the application code five minutes after this migration runs, does the previous code version still work correctly against the resulting schema?' If the honest answer is no, that's a signal to restructure the release -- typically by running the migration as its own separate deploy step, ahead of and independent from the code that depends on it, so the migration itself can be validated and allowed to soak briefly before the code that relies on it goes out. Defaulting to additive-first changes (add before you remove, keep old and new side by side before consolidating) is what keeps that answer 'yes' for as long as possible.

It's worth being explicit that this doesn't fall out for free the way blue-green's router flip does. Blue-green's near-instant rollback and build-once-promote-the-artifact's byte-for-byte consistency are both genuine, valuable guarantees -- but they apply specifically to the stateless application layer, and nothing about them automatically extends to a stateful backing store just because the same release also happens to touch one. A rollback plan for a release that includes a database migration has to be designed on purpose, phase by phase, with contract deliberately deferred until confidence is earned -- it is not a guarantee that comes bundled in with the rest of the deployment pipeline's other, unrelated safety properties.

examples.title: A Rollback That Breaks Because of an Already-Applied Migration
examples.code:
-- Migration applied as part of the release:
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL;

-- New application code (v42) populates it on every insert:
-- INSERT INTO orders (id, price_cents) VALUES (?, ?)

-- Bug found in v42 (unrelated to price_cents). Team rolls back to v41.
-- v41's insert statement predates this column and doesn't set it:
-- INSERT INTO orders (id) VALUES (?)

-- Result: every insert from the rolled-back v41 now fails --
-- ERROR: null value in column "price_cents" violates not-null constraint
examples.explanation: The migration adding `price_cents` as `NOT NULL` with no default was applied once, as part of deploying v42, and rolling back the application code to v41 does not also roll back that schema change -- there is no mechanism that would. v41's insert statement was written and tested before this column existed, so it never populates it, but the constraint added by the migration doesn't know or care which application version is currently running; it rejects any insert missing a required value. The rollback, intended purely as a safe fallback to a previously-working version, is what directly causes this new failure -- the previous code was never actually broken on its own, it's simply now running against a schema it was never designed to satisfy.

examples.title: Expand-Contract in Practice, Phase by Phase
examples.code:
-- EXPAND: add the new column as nullable; no data or old column removed
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN price_cents INTEGER NULL;
-- app code updated to dual-write: both `price` (legacy) and `price_cents` (new)
-- background job backfills price_cents for historical rows

-- MIGRATE: new app code reads price_cents preferentially, falling back to price
-- if for some reason it's still null; old code, if rolled back to, still works
-- fine because `price` is untouched and still being kept correct

-- CONTRACT: only after a soak period with no rollback need --
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN price_cents SET NOT NULL;
ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN price;
-- from this point on, old code that only knows about `price` can no longer
-- run correctly against this schema -- rollback of code alone is no longer safe
examples.explanation: During the expand and migrate phases, a rollback to the previous application version remains genuinely safe, because the schema still contains everything the previous version needs (`price`, still populated by the dual-write). This is precisely the property the earlier broken example was missing -- there, the equivalent of an expand phase (adding the column nullable, dual-writing) was skipped entirely, jumping straight to what's effectively a contract-phase constraint (`NOT NULL`, no fallback) in the very same migration that introduced the column. Only in the contract phase, once `price` is actually dropped, does the safety net finally close -- which is exactly why contract should be delayed until real confidence has been established through the migrate phase running successfully for some time, not treated as an immediate next step after expand.

examples.title: Choosing Roll-Forward When Rollback Would Cause Data Loss
examples.code:
Timeline:
1. Migration drops legacy `email_lowercase` column and rewrites all rows to
   store only normalized `email` going forward. (destructive -- old column gone)
2. New application code deployed, relying entirely on `email`.
3. A bug is discovered: password reset emails are being sent to the wrong
   address for accounts with certain email formats.
4. Team considers rolling back to the previous application version.
5. Previous version's code still reads `email_lowercase`, which no longer
   exists -- rollback would immediately break every account lookup.
6. Decision: roll FORWARD. Ship a targeted patch to the current (new) code
   that fixes the email-matching bug directly, rather than reverting.
examples.explanation: By the time the bug is discovered, the migration has already passed its contract phase -- the legacy column is gone, and there is no version of 'redeploy the old code' that would work, since that old code's fundamental assumption about the schema is no longer true. Attempting the rollback anyway wouldn't just fail to fix anything; it would immediately break account lookups for every user, a considerably worse outage than the original bug. Roll-forward is the only realistic option left: the team accepts that reverting isn't available, and instead writes, reviews, and ships a small, targeted fix on top of the current schema and code -- slower to prepare than a rollback would have been if it were still available, but the only path that doesn't make the situation worse. This is exactly the scenario a rollback plan review, done before step 1 ever shipped, should have flagged: dropping `email_lowercase` in the same release that started depending entirely on `email` closed the rollback door earlier than necessary.

misconceptions.description: If code rollback is fast and mechanical -- for example, in a blue-green setup where it's just flipping a router -- then the entire release is safely reversible.
misconceptions.clarification: Blue-green's speed and mechanical simplicity is real, but it applies specifically to the stateless application layer: the previous artifact is still fully running and untouched, so redirecting traffic to it is genuinely instant. Whether the *release as a whole* is reversible depends on an entirely separate question -- whether any database migration involved is still in a compatible phase (expand or migrate) or has already reached contract, with destructive changes applied. A fast, mechanical code-level rollback mechanism does nothing to undo an already-applied, already-destructive schema change; the two are independent properties of the release, and having one does not imply the other.

misconceptions.description: The expand-contract pattern just means you do a slightly slower version of a normal migration, going through the motions of expand, migrate, and contract quickly back to back.
misconceptions.clarification: The value of the pattern comes specifically from how long the window between the migrate phase and the contract phase is deliberately kept open -- that gap is what preserves the ability to roll back application code safely, since both old and new schema elements coexist for as long as that window lasts. Rushing straight from expand to contract, with no meaningful soak period in between, defeats the pattern's entire purpose: the rollback safety net closes the moment contract runs, so contracting too early leaves a release no safer than a naive, single-step migration would have been, just with extra steps that were never actually given time to pay off.

exercises.prompt: This release plan adds a required column and deploys code that depends on it in a single step. The team was recently burned when a rollback attempt failed because of exactly this pattern. Find the specific problem and propose a fix using the phases described in this concept.
exercises.code:
-- Single migration, deployed together with the new application code:
ALTER TABLE subscriptions ADD COLUMN renewal_period TEXT NOT NULL;
-- New app code writes renewal_period on every insert/update.
-- Old app code (the rollback target) never sets this column at all.
hints: If the team needed to roll back the application code five minutes after this migration ran, would the old code's inserts/updates still succeed against this schema?
The column is added as NOT NULL with no default in the very same step that starts depending on it -- compare this to the expand phase described in the concept, which adds new columns nullable first.
Split this into phases: add the column nullable (expand) and have both old and new code paths tolerate its absence for a while, THEN make it NOT NULL only after confidence is established (contract).
exercises.solutionCode:
-- EXPAND (this release): add nullable, no dependency yet
ALTER TABLE subscriptions ADD COLUMN renewal_period TEXT NULL;
-- New app code writes renewal_period when available, but tolerates it being
-- null (e.g. falls back to a default period) -- so old code, which never sets
-- it, does not violate any constraint if rollback is needed here.

-- MIGRATE (later release, after this one has soaked): app code now relies on
-- renewal_period more fully, backfilled for historical rows.

-- CONTRACT (still later, after further confidence): only now --
ALTER TABLE subscriptions ALTER COLUMN renewal_period SET NOT NULL;
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original plan collapses expand and contract into a single step: the column is both introduced and immediately made mandatory in the same migration that the new code starts depending on, which means a rollback to the previous code -- which never sets this column -- would violate the `NOT NULL` constraint on every write, exactly as in the worked example in this concept. The fix separates the phases: this release only expands (adds the column nullable, with application code tolerant of it being absent), which keeps the previous code version fully rollback-safe, since nothing about the schema yet requires what old code doesn't provide. The `NOT NULL` constraint is deferred to a later, separate release, made only once the column has been reliably populated for a while and there's real confidence a rollback won't be needed -- at which point tightening the constraint is a much lower-risk, deliberate contract step rather than an accidental one bundled into the original change.

exercises.prompt: A migration destructively drops a column and rewrites historical data in a way that cannot be reconstructed from what remains. A bug is then found in the new code. What happens if the team attempts a standard rollback to the previous application version, and what should they do instead?
exercises.code:
-- Migration (already applied):
ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN legacy_region_code;
-- historical rows also rewritten -- legacy_region_code values are gone, not
-- derivable from any other stored column

-- Previous app version's code:
-- SELECT legacy_region_code FROM users WHERE id = ?
hints: Does the column the old code depends on still exist in the schema at all, after this migration?
Rolling back is only a safe option if the previous code's assumptions about the schema still hold -- check whether that's true here.
When a migration has already destroyed information a rollback target depends on, what's the only remaining path that doesn't risk making things worse?
exercises.expectedAnswer: Rolling back would fail immediately -- every query in the old code referencing legacy_region_code would error, since the column no longer exists at all. Because the drop was destructive and the data isn't recoverable from what remains, rollback is not a real option; the team must roll forward, shipping a targeted fix on top of the current schema and code instead of reverting.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The previous application version's queries reference `legacy_region_code` directly, and that column has been physically removed from the schema -- there is nothing to fall back to; every such query would fail with a missing-column error the instant the old code ran. This is a case where the migration has already passed the point where code-level rollback could help at all, regardless of how fast or mechanical the deployment tooling's rollback mechanism otherwise is. The only viable path is roll-forward: keep the current (buggy but at least schema-compatible) code running, and ship a specific, reviewed fix for the actual bug on top of it, accepting that reverting is off the table once a migration has destroyed information a prior version depended on.

assessments.prompt: A team's deploy pipeline can redeploy any previous artifact in under a minute. During an incident following a release that included a database migration, this fast redeploy mechanism turns out not to fix the problem. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The deploy pipeline itself is broken and needs to be fixed before rollback can work at all.
The migration has already changed the schema in a way the previous application version is not compatible with, so redeploying old code doesn't undo the schema change and may itself cause new errors.
Rollback mechanisms only work for frontend code, never for backend services with a database.
The team should have used a canary deployment instead of whatever strategy they used.
assessments.explanation: A fast, working artifact-redeploy mechanism addresses only the stateless application layer -- it says nothing about whether the database's current schema is still compatible with the code being redeployed. If the migration already ran and changed the schema in a way the old code doesn't expect (a new required column it never populates, a dropped column it still queries), redeploying that old code can fail or actively cause new errors, entirely independent of how fast or reliable the redeploy mechanism itself is. Option A misdiagnoses a schema-compatibility problem as a pipeline problem; option C is a false, overly broad claim -- rollback absolutely can work for backend services, just not unconditionally once state is involved; option D conflates a different release strategy choice with the specific rollback-compatibility issue being described here.

assessments.prompt: A team's migration adds a new NOT NULL column with no default in the same step that the new application code starts depending on it, with no separate expand phase beforehand. According to this concept, what specifically goes wrong if a rollback to the previous application version is needed shortly afterward?
options: Nothing goes wrong -- rollback works fine as long as the previous code doesn't reference the new column by name anywhere.

The previous code's inserts and updates, written before the column existed, never populate it, but the NOT NULL constraint still applies regardless of which code version is running -- so the rollback itself causes every write to start failing, on code that was previously running fine.
The rollback would succeed without issue, but only if performed within five minutes of the original deploy.
This is only a problem for columns added to tables that already contain existing rows; brand-new, empty tables are unaffected.
assessments.explanation: This is precisely the worked example in this concept: adding `price_cents` as NOT NULL with no default, in the same step the new code starts depending on it, means a rollback to code that never populates the column violates the constraint on every insert -- turning the intended safe fallback into a new outage. Option A ignores that the constraint applies at the database level regardless of what the rolled-back code references. Option C invents an arbitrary time window that has no bearing on constraint enforcement. Option D is false -- the constraint applies to every new write regardless of whether the table had prior rows.

assessments.prompt: A migration has already dropped a column that the previous application version's queries directly reference, with the underlying data not reconstructable from anything else stored. A new, unrelated bug is then found in the current code. According to this concept, what is the recommended response?
options: Roll back to the previous application version immediately, since rollback is always the safer and faster option regardless of what the migration already did.

Roll forward -- ship a targeted fix on top of the current schema and code, since reverting to a version whose queries reference a column that no longer exists would fail immediately and could cause a second, likely worse, incident.
Restore the entire database from a backup taken before the migration ran, since this is always a safe, low-risk operation to perform.
Wait for the bug to resolve itself, since both rollback and roll-forward are considered too risky in this specific scenario.
assessments.explanation: The concept works through exactly this scenario: once a migration has destroyed information a rollback target depends on, reverting isn't a real option at all, and roll-forward -- a targeted fix on the current, schema-compatible code -- is the only realistic path. Option A ignores that rollback here would break every account lookup outright. Option C treats a backup restore as risk-free, when the concept notes it carries its own risk of losing other data written since. Option D incorrectly implies no safe path exists, when roll-forward is explicitly presented as viable.

assessments.prompt: Before shipping a release that includes both application code and a database migration, this concept recommends asking a specific diagnostic question in advance. What is it?
options: 'How many total lines of code changed across this entire release?'
'If we need to roll back the application code five minutes after this migration runs, does the previous code version still work correctly against the resulting schema?'
'Which specific team member is responsible for formally approving this deploy?'
'Is this release scheduled to go out during a low-traffic time window?'
assessments.explanation: The concept states this question explicitly as the practical discipline to apply before any release involving a schema change -- if the honest answer is no, that's a signal to restructure the release, typically by running the migration as its own separate, additive-first step. Option A measures diff size, which the broader subject explicitly treats as unrelated to compatibility risk. Option C and D raise process and scheduling questions that don't address whether rollback itself remains safe.

assessments.prompt: You're planning a release that both changes application code and requires a database migration adding a new required piece of data. Explain, in concrete terms, how you would sequence the release so that a rollback remains genuinely safe for as long as possible, and under what condition you'd accept that rollback is no longer available.
assessments.modelAnswer: I'd deliberately avoid shipping the migration and the code that depends on it as a single atomic release, because that collapses expand and contract into one step and immediately removes any rollback safety net -- if the previous code doesn't know about the new required data, a rollback to it would violate whatever constraint the migration just added, turning the 'safe fallback' into a second incident. Instead, I'd sequence it in phases. First, an expand-only release: add the new column or field as nullable, with the new application code writing to it but tolerating its absence (falling back to a default, or simply leaving it null) if the previous version is still in play or a rollback happens to this phase. At this point, both the previous and the new application versions can run correctly against the schema, so rolling back is fully safe. Second, once that expand release has soaked for a reasonable period with no need to roll back, I'd ship a migrate release: application code that now depends more fully on the new field, with historical data backfilled -- rollback to the pre-expand version is no longer relevant at this point, but rollback to the expand-phase version remains safe, since the column is still there and still populated. Only after that has also soaked with confidence would I ship a contract release that actually tightens the constraint (making the field required at the database level) and removes whatever old fallback path or old column it's replacing. I would treat rollback as no longer available specifically once that contract step has run -- from that point on, redeploying any version of the code that predates the constraint being enforced, or that depends on something the contract step removed, is not a safe fallback anymore, and if a serious bug is found after contracting, the right response is a targeted roll-forward fix rather than attempting to revert. The core discipline throughout is treating 'is a rollback still safe right now' as a question with a genuinely different, and changing, answer at each phase, rather than assuming the deploy pipeline's general rollback speed for stateless code automatically extends to cover the database changes riding along with it.
